title: Increasing susceptibility to priming of soil N mineralisation across a subarctic tundra‐forest ecotone under N fertilisation
content:

Abstract

Climate change is driving shrub encroachment and treeline advance in the Arctic, increasing inputs of plant-derived carbon (C) to soil. These inputs could enhance or reduce microbial decomposition of soil organic matter (SOM) (‘priming’), affecting the soil C balance. In nitrogen (N)-poor subarctic soils, priming may arise due to selective microbial N-mining. We investigated the susceptibility of soils to priming across a subarctic ecotone (four sites: birch forest, treeline, shrub-dominated tundra, tundra heath). Fertilisation with N and phosphorus (P) in the field for 2 years was used to test how nutrient availability interacted with plant communities to modulate microbial responses to simulated rhizosphere input. Soils were incubated with either 13C-glucose (simulating rhizosphere input) or water (control) for 1 week under controlled laboratory conditions to assess priming effects on soil C mineralisation, soil N mineralisation and microbial growth. Soil and foliar nutrient concentrations tended to decline from forest to tundra, reflecting shifts in vegetation composition and associated plant–soil-microbial feedbacks. Soil C mineralisation was initially primed most strongly in tundra (+130%) and P-fertilised treeline soils (+150%), but these effects largely disappeared within 24 h, resulting in no change to the overall soil C balance. In all soils, in the absence of added glucose, we found evidence for selective microbial use of N-rich organic matter, suggesting high microbial demand for N. However, counter to expectation, glucose addition did not generally strengthen selective microbial N-mining, likely because microbial use of N-rich SOM was already near its stoichiometric limit (set by the lowest possible C:N ratio of organic compounds). This was with the exception of N-fertilised soils, where glucose addition primed soil N mineralisation (up to +250%), resulting in intensified selective microbial N-mining, with an effect size that tended to strengthen towards the forest. Microbial growth peaked 1 day after glucose addition and was then sustained, with stronger responses in fertilised soils, consistent with alleviated nutrient limitation. We show that in subarctic soils, priming of N mineralisation is regulated by N availability, suggesting contrasting feedbacks depending on soil nutrient status. In more N-poor tundra soils, labile C inputs may slow N cycling and further reduce N availability. In comparably fertile treeline and forest soils, labile C inputs may instead accelerate N cycling, increasing inorganic N availability to plants.
